title: Proverbs
intro: 31 days through Proverbs, one short passage from each chapter.

posts.caption: Starting today, 31 days through Proverbs, one short passage from each chapter. Proverbs is Hebrew wisdom literature, practical sayings about living well, traditionally linked to King Solomon. This verse is the book's motto: real wisdom starts with reverence for God, and refusing to learn is what makes a fool. "Fear of the LORD" means reverence and awe, not terror. With exactly 31 chapters, it's a popular book to read a chapter a day for a month.

Chapters 1 to 9 are framed as a parent teaching a child ("my son"). In Hebrew, much of chapter 2 is one long sentence: if you search for wisdom like silver or hidden treasure, then you will find it. This verse gives the reason. In Proverbs, wisdom takes effort to seek, yet in the end it is a gift from God.

Perhaps the best-loved lines in Proverbs, part of a parent's advice to a child. The point is wholehearted trust: relying on God rather than on one's own judgment alone, and bringing God into every part of life. In Hebrew thought the "heart" is the center of thinking and choosing, not only feeling, and "acknowledge" is literally "know." "Make your paths straight" can also mean smooth or level, like a road cleared for a traveler.

Just before this, the father recalls being taught by his own father (verse 4), so three generations stand behind the advice. "Heart" again means the whole inner life: thoughts, desires and choices. The image is of a spring that must be protected, because everything else flows out of it.

posts.display: May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth.
posts.caption: Chapter 5 warns a young man against adultery, then turns to praise faithful married love. Just before this line, the poem pictures that love as drinking from one's own well, a precious thing in a dry land, and the "fountain" carries on the same image. "The wife of your youth" is a tender phrase for a lifelong partner; the prophet Malachi uses it too.

Proverbs often draws lessons from nature. The "slacker" (the old "sluggard") is one of the book's stock characters, and here he is sent to learn from the ant, which plans ahead and stores food without anyone giving orders. The lesson is diligence that doesn't need a boss. Harvester ants, common in Israel, really do gather seeds and store them in their nests. A few verses later comes a famous warning: "A little sleep, a little slumber..."

A parent urges a child to treasure wise teaching and keep it close, until it becomes part of who they are. "Apple of your eye" means the pupil, which people instinctively protect; the Hebrew word, ishon, literally means "little man," probably from the tiny reflection seen in another's eye. Tying teachings to the fingers echoes Deuteronomy 6, the basis of the Jewish practice of wearing tefillin. The chapter goes on to tell of a young man lured by an adulteress.

In chapters 1 to 9, Wisdom is pictured as a woman, Lady Wisdom, who calls out at the city gates. Her claim is simple: wisdom is worth more than any treasure, so choose her over silver and gold. The Hebrew word translated "rubies," peninim, may instead mean corals or pearls. Later in this chapter she says she was beside God at creation, an idea Jewish tradition linked with the Torah and early Christians with Christ.

Chapter 9 ends the opening section with two rival invitations: Lady Wisdom sets a feast in her house, and a woman named Folly calls out to the same passersby. The choice between them sums up everything so far: wisdom offers a solid, well-built life, folly a dead end. Seven was a number of completeness, so seven pillars suggests a large, perfect house. T. E. Lawrence ("Lawrence of Arabia") took the title of his memoir, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, from this verse.

Chapter 10 begins a new collection headed "The proverbs of Solomon," made mostly of two-line sayings. Many work by contrast, joined by "but." To "cover" wrongs here means not exposing them or stirring them up again. The New Testament letter 1 Peter echoes this verse: "love covers over a multitude of sins."

Proverbs often notices that generosity comes back around. "A generous soul" is literally "a soul of blessing," and the second line in Hebrew is a picture of water: one who waters others will be watered, a vivid image in a dry land. Like most proverbs, it describes how life tends to go rather than making a guarantee.

A lesser-known proverb about animals. The Hebrew literally says a righteous person "knows the soul" of his animal: its life and needs. The Torah also commands care for animals, including a Sabbath rest for working livestock. The second line is wry: even what the wicked call mercy turns out to be cruelty.

An honest observation about waiting. "Tree of life" recalls the tree in the Garden of Eden. Proverbs uses the phrase four times: for wisdom, for the fruit of righteousness, here for a longing fulfilled, and for gentle words. It pictures the deep refreshment of a hope finally met.

Proverbs ties how people treat the poor to how they treat God. Because God made rich and poor alike (as 22:2 says), exploiting the poor is pictured as an insult to their Maker. Jesus makes a similar connection in Matthew 25: "whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me."

One of the most quoted proverbs. Speech is among the book's favorite subjects: how words can calm or inflame, heal or wound. In Hebrew, a "harsh word" is literally a "word of pain," one that hurts. Another proverb makes the same point with a paradox: "a gentle tongue can break a bone" (25:15).

Proverbs warns again and again that arrogance sets people up for ruin, and this is its most famous version, the source of the English saying "pride goes before a fall." "Haughty" in Hebrew is literally "high": a lofty spirit has further to fall. Chapter 16 also has many sayings about human plans and God's purposes, such as: "A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps."

Friendship is one of Proverbs' favorite subjects. One common reading of this verse: a friend's love is constant, and a brother shows his true worth when trouble comes. Others read the second line as a step further: in hard times, a real friend becomes like family. Either way, adversity reveals loyalty.

In ancient cities, a fortified tower was the strongest point of the walls, the place people ran to when attackers came. Proverbs pictures God as that place of safety for those who live rightly. In the Bible, a "name" stands for a person's character and presence, so running to the name means trusting God himself. The very next verse offers a contrast: the rich man thinks his wealth is a high wall, but only "in his imagination."

Proverbs praises careful planning and good advice, and also holds that God's purposes have the final word. The Hebrew contrasts a person's "many plans" with God's single purpose, which literally "will stand." Similar sayings appear in 16:9 and 21:30, part of a running theme in the book.

Not every proverb is lofty; some are sharp snapshots of everyday life. Here, a haggler in an ancient market. In Hebrew he says simply "Bad, bad!" to talk down the price, then walks away bragging about his bargain. The proverb doesn't spell out a moral; it simply holds up a mirror.

This saying echoes the Hebrew prophets, who insisted that worship without justice was empty. Hosea quotes God: "I desire mercy, not sacrifice," and Micah sums up what God requires as acting justly, loving mercy and walking humbly. Since sacrifice was at the heart of temple worship, this was a striking claim.

One of the most famous proverbs: habits formed in childhood tend to last a lifetime, so shaping a child well matters. It's also a good example of how the book works: proverbs are general observations about how life usually goes, not promises or guarantees. "In the way he should go" is literally "according to his way" in Hebrew, which some interpreters read as training suited to each child's own nature.

A warning against wearing yourself out to get rich: wealth is fleeting and can vanish as suddenly as a bird takes flight. This comes from a section introduced as "thirty sayings" (22:20). Many scholars think it draws on an Egyptian text, the Instruction of Amenemope, which is also divided into thirty chapters and also pictures riches growing wings like geese and flying to the sky. Israel's sages seem to have adapted wisdom from their neighbors.

Seven is the Bible's number of completeness, so "seven times" means again and again. The point is not that the righteous never fall, but that they keep getting up, while for the wicked one stumble is enough. The verse is addressed to a wicked man plotting against a righteous neighbor: his victim will rise again.

The right word at the right moment is a thing of beauty, pictured here as golden fruit, probably a piece of jewelry, in a silver setting. Proverbs prizes not only what is said but when. Chapter 25 opens a new collection, proverbs of Solomon "copied by the men of Hezekiah," a king of Judah around 700 BC, a rare glimpse of how the book was gathered and edited over centuries.

These two proverbs sit side by side and seem to contradict each other. That's the point: wisdom means knowing which one fits the moment. The Talmud records that some ancient rabbis, troubled by such contradictions, considered withdrawing Proverbs from use, until they concluded that each verse applies to a different kind of situation.

Iron blades were sharpened against iron. The Hebrew literally says one person sharpens "the face" of another, perhaps meaning their wits or character. It pictures friends improving each other through honest, even abrasive, exchange. Earlier in the chapter: "The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful."

Hiding wrongdoing gets a person nowhere, the proverb says, but owning up and turning away from it opens the door to mercy. In Hebrew, "conceals" is the same verb as "covers" in 10:12, where love covers transgressions: covering someone else's offense can be an act of love, but covering one's own is hiding. In both Jewish and Christian traditions, confessing and turning from wrongdoing are at the heart of repentance.

This verse is often quoted about leadership and goals, from the older translation "Where there is no vision, the people perish." But the Hebrew word for vision, hazon, means prophetic revelation, a message from God. Without it, the verse says, a people "cast off restraint," and the second line points to God's law as the guide.

Chapter 30 is credited to Agur son of Jakeh, who is otherwise unknown. He uses a numerical pattern, "three things... four," also found in the prophet Amos. What links these four is debated: perhaps each moves in a mysterious way, or leaves no trail to follow. The last, a man with a maiden, seems to point to the mystery of love.

The book closes with a 22-verse acrostic poem praising the "woman of valor" (eshet chayil in Hebrew): strong, capable and generous. Its final point is that charm and looks fade, but a woman who reveres God deserves praise, which brings the book back to its motto, the fear of the LORD. Many Jewish families sing the poem at the Friday night Sabbath table. That's Proverbs, one chapter at a time. Thank you for reading it with me.
